provenance: Agent-curated summaries of linked original sources; not Papiers search results, not human annotations, and not Toronto-calibrated forecast parameters.

papers.title: Bloor Street West Bike Lane Pilot Project Evaluation
papers.authors: City of Toronto, General Manager, Transportation Services
papers.finding: Pilot area cycling rose 49% (3,309 to 4,925 per day; 25% of the increase estimated as new riders) while Harbord fell 25% and Dupont 11%; Bloor motor vehicles fell 16%, net across three corridors -3%; peak travel times rose 0:32 to 4:15 after signal adjustments; on-street parking 303 to 167 spaces (total -10%); conflicts -44% overall but bike-pedestrian +61%; Moneris spending grew 4.45% in pilot area vs 3.73% surrounding, 2.21% Danforth, 4.96% city-wide; 57% of drivers who do not bike and 51% of business respondents disagreed with the trade-off.
papers.mvp_use: Primary Toronto baseline for installation effects, diversion branches, parking supply and a real stakeholder-opinion split for personas.
papers.transfer_limit: Installation in 2016-2017, observational before/after, under one year of collision data; removal in 2026 may not reverse these effects symmetrically.

papers.title: Economic Impact Study of Bike Lanes in Toronto's Bloor Annex and Korea Town Neighbourhoods
papers.authors: Nancy Smith Lea; Yvonne Verlinden; Beth Savan; Daniel Arancibia; Steven Farber; Lee Vernich; Jeff Allen
papers.finding: 3,005 visitor surveys, 525 merchant surveys and 15 bike counts across fall 2015, fall 2016 and spring 2017; more merchants reported 100+ customers, visitors reported higher spending and three more visit days per month, vacancies stable at 6%; but the same indicators also grew on the Danforth control, so positive outcomes may be attributable to other factors.
papers.mvp_use: Survey instrument template (merchant Q1 customer counts, Q6 estimated customer mode shares) and evidence that walking/cycling visitors visit more often.
papers.transfer_limit: Commissioned by the BIAs, City and Metcalf Foundation and written by an active-transportation organization; self-reported survey indicators; Danforth control later received cycle tracks in 2020. Report says the vacancy rate was 6%; the City staff report says 7%.

papers.title: Measuring the Local Economic Impacts of Replacing On-Street Parking With Bike Lanes: A Toronto (Canada) Case Study
papers.journal: Journal of the American Planning Association 85(4): 463-481
papers.finding: Peer-reviewed publication of the B02 Bloor study.
papers.mvp_use: Cite as the peer-reviewed version of B02 when a human checks the paper itself.
papers.transfer_limit: Same data and limits as B02.

papers.title: Bike Lanes, On-Street Parking and Business: Year 2 Report (Bloor West Village)
papers.authors: Jennifer Forkes; Nancy Smith Lea (Clean Air Partnership)
papers.finding: 96 merchants and 510 visitors: 21% of visitors usually drove, but 69% of merchants believed more than 20% of customers drove; 46% of merchants expected a bike lane with 50% less parking to decrease customers (Annex 2008: 25%); non-drivers visited more often and reported spending more per month.
papers.mvp_use: Initialize merchant personas with a measured belief gap and let the survey/skeptic challenge it; heterogeneity between neighbourhoods.
papers.transfer_limit: Stated perceptions and intercept surveys, no actual sales data; Bloor West Village has a different street width and more driving than the Annex.

papers.title: Bike Lanes, On-Street Parking and Business: A Study of Bloor Street in Toronto's Annex Neighbourhood
papers.finding: 2008 survey of 61 merchants and 538 patrons on Bloor in the Annex: 46% walked, 32% transit, 12% cycled, 10% drove; merchants' mode estimates were broadly accurate and more expected a lane to help than hurt.
papers.mvp_use: Pre-pilot customer mode share for the Annex shop personas; contrast with B04 where merchants overestimated driving.
papers.transfer_limit: 2008 data, one summer survey; summarized from secondary sources and the B04 comparison tables.

papers.title: Economic impacts on local businesses of investments in bicycle and pedestrian infrastructure: a review of the evidence
papers.authors: Jamey M. B. Volker; Susan Handy
papers.finding: Review of 23 mostly US/Canadian studies: active-travel facilities generally have positive or non-significant effects on retail and food-service businesses, while bicycle facilities may hurt auto-oriented businesses.
papers.mvp_use: Business-type heterogeneity: give an auto-oriented shop persona a different response than a cafe.
papers.transfer_limit: Literature review of installations with mixed designs; not a removal estimate.

papers.title: Understanding Economic and Business Impacts of Street Improvements for Bicycle and Pedestrian Mobility: A Multi-City Multi-Approach Exploration
papers.finding: Fourteen corridors in six US cities: street improvements had positive or no significant effects on corridor business performance; food service gained most.
papers.mvp_use: Low/base/high retail cases that include zero.
papers.transfer_limit: US cities, installation not removal; co-sponsored by PeopleForBikes.

papers.title: Vancouver Separated Bike Lane Business Impact Study
papers.finding: Estimated sales declines of about 10% on Hornby and 4% on Dunsmuir, largely from business-reported perceptions, with about one-third survey participation and hot-spot blocks.
papers.mvp_use: Required negative retail case for the sweep and the skeptic.
papers.transfer_limit: Perception-based, low response, confounded by 2010 Olympics, HST and downtown construction; primary PDF could not be downloaded, so figures come from secondary summaries.

papers.title: Route Infrastructure and the Risk of Injuries to Bicyclists: A Case-Crossover Study
papers.finding: 690 injured adult cyclists in Toronto and Vancouver: cycle tracks had the lowest risk, adjusted OR 0.11 (95% CI 0.02-0.54) relative to major streets with parked cars and no bike infrastructure.
papers.mvp_use: Safety branch with a wide uncertainty range; cited in B01.
papers.transfer_limit: Relative injury odds by route type, not a predicted collision count for Bloor after removal.

papers.title: Bikeway Networks: A Review of Effects on Cycling
papers.finding: Most studies find a positive relationship between bikeway networks and cycling; stated and revealed preferences favour separated facilities; network-level evidence is thin.
papers.mvp_use: Supports a separated-lane preference in cyclist personas and a reroute branch on removal.
papers.transfer_limit: Review of associations; no removal elasticity.

papers.title: City staff report on provincially ordered removal of Bloor, Yonge and University bike lanes (Bill 212)
papers.finding: Staff estimated removal at $48 million or more and expected minimal travel-time improvement once lanes are removed, with multi-season reconstruction on Bloor between Spadina and Avenue Rd.
papers.mvp_use: Public-budget ledger and construction-disruption ticks for the removal scenario.
papers.transfer_limit: Reported through news coverage; primary staff report not retrieved. Province disputed the cost.

policy_context.title: Cycle Toronto v. Ontario (Attorney General), 2026 ONCA 582
policy_context.summary: Court of Appeal allowed the province's appeal of the 30 July 2025 Superior Court ruling; there is no Charter right to bicycle lanes, so removal under Bill 212 may proceed.
policy_context.use: Context for why the question is live; not causal evidence.

conflicts.caveat: B02's own control street improved similarly; most designs are weak. Run negative, zero and positive retail cases.
Belief accuracy differs by neighbourhood; do not hard-code one merchant bias.
All economic evidence is from installation; removal may differ because riders, routes and businesses adapted since 2016.

parameter_gate: Observed corridor facts load from data/bloor_bike_lane_baseline.json. Reroute, mode-switch, customer-loss and business-response values are sensitivity cases with source IDs and human approval, never Toronto forecasts.
